A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities and countries that work together to deliver websites, videos, and apps quickly to people everywhere. Without one, every request for a piece of content would travel all the way back to a single origin server, which is the original computer where a website's files are permanently stored. That trip can be slow, especially for someone far away. A CDN solves this by placing copies of that content on many smaller computers called edge locations, servers positioned closer to where people actually are, in cities around the world. When someone requests a page, the network checks whether a nearby edge location already holds a saved copy; if it does, that is called a cache hit, meaning the content is delivered instantly from the nearby location instead of the distant original. Think of it like a chain of bakeries that all sell bread baked at one central factory; instead of everyone driving across the country to the factory each morning, local branches keep fresh loaves ready nearby, so customers get bread faster. Only when a branch runs out, or the bread is new, does a fresh delivery from the factory become necessary. This arrangement keeps things running smoothly during busy periods, reduces strain on the original computer, and helps everything stay available even if one location has trouble, since traffic simply shifts to another nearby spot instead.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | It is the ultimate source; too many direct requests can slow it down |
| Edge location | A smaller server placed near a group of people | It shortens the distance content has to travel, making delivery faster |
| Cache hit | A request answered by a saved nearby copy | It means near-instant delivery without contacting the origin server |
| Latency | The delay between asking for content and receiving it | Lower delay makes videos, pages, and apps feel smooth and responsive |
